title: Resolution 827: The Court That Would Judge a War
content:
On 25 May 1993, the United Nations Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 827, formally establishing the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. It was the first international war crimes tribunal created since the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals of the 1940s, and the first ever established by the Security Council acting under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. The ICTY would go on to fundamentally reshape international criminal law, but at the moment of its creation, its significance was far from certain.

The legal groundwork had been laid months earlier. Resolution 808, adopted on 22 February 1993, had expressed the Council's decision to establish a tribunal and requested the Secretary-General to prepare a report with specific proposals. The resulting report (S/25704) outlined the tribunal's statute, jurisdiction, and organizational structure. The ICTY was granted authority over four categories of offenses committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991: grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, violations of the laws or customs of war, genocide, and crimes against humanity. Its jurisdiction was concurrent with national courts but with primacy -- meaning it could claim cases from domestic legal systems.

The political context of the tribunal's creation was as important as its legal architecture. By May 1993, the evidence of systematic atrocities in Bosnia-Herzegovina was overwhelming. Reports of concentration camps, mass executions, systematic sexual violence, and the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure had been accumulating since the summer of 1992. The UN Commission of Experts, established by Resolution 780 in October 1992, had been gathering testimony and documentation that confirmed patterns of grave violations across the conflict. The creation of the ICTY was, in part, a response to growing international public pressure to act -- and an acknowledgment that the existing diplomatic and peacekeeping frameworks had failed to prevent or halt the violence.

Critics noted from the outset that establishing a court was not the same as stopping a war. The tribunal had no police force, no power to arrest suspects, and depended entirely on the cooperation of states and international organizations for the execution of its orders. Its first prosecutor would not be appointed until August 1994, and the first indictments would follow only after that. For the populations under siege in Sarajevo, Srebrenica, and Gorazde, the creation of a court in The Hague offered little immediate relief.

The Bosnian government cautiously welcomed the tribunal's establishment as an acknowledgment that crimes were being committed and that accountability would eventually follow. For Bosniak political leaders, the ICTY represented at least the possibility that the international community's response to the war would extend beyond humanitarian aid and ineffective ceasefire negotiations. However, there was also skepticism that the tribunal would ever have the capacity or political support to bring senior leaders to justice.

The Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat leaderships received the news with varying degrees of public dismissiveness and private concern. The creation of a tribunal with jurisdiction over their commanders and political officials introduced a new variable into wartime calculations -- one whose consequences were difficult to predict but potentially severe.

The ICTY's eventual record would prove substantial. Over its twenty-four-year lifespan, the tribunal indicted 161 individuals, concluded proceedings against 111 accused, and produced a body of jurisprudence that advanced the law of genocide, command responsibility, and sexual violence as a weapon of war. Its factual findings, preserved in thousands of pages of trial judgments, constitute the most comprehensive judicial record of any armed conflict in history. But all of that lay in the future. In May 1993, the tribunal existed only on paper -- a statement of intent by an international community that had yet to demonstrate the will to enforce it.
